extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students and instructors (real analysis / advanced calculus)
extracted.subtask_description: Chapter-level textbook exposition of the Riemann (Darboux) integral: definitions, necessary/sufficient criteria for integrability, key properties (additivity, linearity, monotonicity), and common examples/counterexamples. Intended to teach how to determine when a bounded function on an interval is Riemann integrable and how to compute its integral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partition of an interval
rubrics_metrics.description: A partition P of [a,b] is a finite set of numbers x0, x1, x2, ..., xn with a = x0 < x1 < x2 < ... < xn = b.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the basic combinatorial object used to define Darboux sums; refinements of partitions (adding more points) are used to make upper and lower sums closer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lower and upper Darboux sums (L_{P,f}, U_{P,f})
rubrics_metrics.description: For a bounded function f on [a,b] and a partition P with subintervals [x_{i-1}, x_i], set m_i = inf_{x in [x_{i-1},x_i]} f(x) and M_i = sup_{x in [x_{i-1},x_i]} f(x). Define L_{P,f} = sum_{i=1}^n m_i Δx_i and U_{P,f} = sum_{i=1}^n M_i Δx_i.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric interpretation: L is area of shaded (min-height) rectangles, U is area of full (max-height) rectangles. These sums provide lower and upper approximations to the 'area under the curve'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lower and upper Darboux integrals (underline and overline integrals)
rubrics_metrics.description: The lower Darboux integral is sup_P L_{P,f} (supremum over all partitions). The upper Darboux integral is inf_P U_{P,f} (infimum over all partitions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These two numbers always exist for bounded f on [a,b] and bound the integral from below and above respectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Riemann integrability criterion (Darboux formulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A bounded function f on [a,b] is Riemann integrable if and only if the lower Darboux integral equals the upper Darboux integral: sup_P L_{P,f} = inf_P U_{P,f}. In that case the common value is the integral ∫_a^b f.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the textbook definition used throughout. Many subsequent criteria and theorems rephrase or provide sufficient conditions for this equality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boundedness prerequisite
rubrics_metrics.description: By definition, the Darboux/Riemann integral is defined only for bounded functions on [a,b]; the sets of lower and upper sums are bounded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposition 5.1.2 shows that if m ≤ f(x) ≤ M on [a,b], then for any partition P, m(b-a) ≤ L_{P,f} ≤ U_{P,f} ≤ M(b-a). So integrability requires boundedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refinement monotonicity of Darboux sums
rubrics_metrics.description: If P' is a refinement of P (i.e., P ⊂ P'), then L_{P,f} ≤ L_{P',f} and U_{P',f} ≤ U_{P,f}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Making partitions finer cannot decrease the lower sums or increase the upper sums; refinements are the main tool for squeezing the two sums together (Proposition 5.1.7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inequality of lower and upper integrals
rubrics_metrics.description: For any bounded f on [a,b], the lower Darboux integral is ≤ the upper Darboux integral (∫_a^b f_lower ≤ ∫_a^b f_upper), and both are sandwiched by m(b-a) and M(b-a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is Proposition 5.1.8. It asserts that the two integrals define a closed interval; integrability is the statement that the interval collapses to a point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epsilon-partition criterion for integrability (Proposition 5.1.13)
rubrics_metrics.description: A bounded function f on [a,b] is Riemann integrable if and only if for every ε > 0 there exists a partition P such that U_{P,f} - L_{P,f} < ε.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practical criterion is commonly used to prove integrability directly: produce partitions making the oscillation-sum arbitrarily small.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integral bounds from pointwise bounds (Proposition 5.1.10)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is Riemann integrable on [a,b] and m ≤ f(x) ≤ M for all x, then m(b-a) ≤ ∫_a^b f ≤ M(b-a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful to estimate integrals and to rule out certain behaviors. Also used to show integrals of constant functions equal constant×length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-integrability example (Dirichlet function)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Dirichlet function f(x)=1 if x∈Q and 0 if x∉Q on [0,1] has L_{P,f}=0 and U_{P,f}=1 for every partition P, hence lower integral 0 and upper integral 1, so not Riemann integrable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serves as canonical counterexample: dense oscillation between two values prevents U-L from shrinking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrability of step/elementary step functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Elementary step functions (indicator of a bounded interval) and finite linear combinations (step functions) are Riemann integrable on any [a,b]; their integrals equal the sum of constants times lengths of intervals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples (5.1.12 and exercises) show how to compute integrals for such simple functions using partitions designed around jump points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additivity over adjacent intervals (Lemma 5.2.1 & Proposition 5.2.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a < b < c and f is bounded, then lower and upper integrals are additive: ∫_a^c f = ∫_a^b f + ∫_b^c f (for both lower and upper integrals). Moreover, f is Riemann integrable on [a,c] iff it is integrable on [a,b] and [b,c], in which case ∫_a^c f = ∫_a^b f + ∫_b^c f.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical rule for computing integrals piecewise and for proving integrability by dividing domain into subintervals where behavior is nicer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linearity of the integral (Proposition 5.2.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f and g are Riemann integrable on [a,b] and α∈ℝ, then αf and f+g are Riemann integrable and ∫_a^b αf = α∫_a^b f and ∫_a^b (f+g) = ∫_a^b f + ∫_a^b g.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For α < 0 one uses the fact that −f integrable implies αf integrable; proofs rely on moving scalars past infima/suprema and exercise-work is provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotonicity of the integral (Proposition 5.2.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f and g are bounded on [a,b] and f(x) ≤ g(x) for all x in [a,b], then lower and upper integrals satisfy ∫_a^b f ≤ ∫_a^b g. If f and g are Riemann integrable then ∫_a^b f ≤ ∫_a^b g.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to compare integrals; follows from comparing infima/suprema on each subinterval and taking sup/inf over partitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous functions are Riemann integrable (Lemma 5.2.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is continuous on the closed bounded interval [a,b], then f is Riemann integrable on [a,b].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses uniform continuity on compact interval: choose partition with subinterval length < δ to make M_i - m_i small, hence U_P - L_P < ε.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrability under controlled discontinuities (Lemma 5.2.8 and Theorem 5.2.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is bounded on [a,b] and integrable on an increasing sequence of closed subintervals [a_n,b_n] with a_n→a and b_n→b and lim ∫_{a_n}^{b_n} f exists, then f is integrable on [a,b] and the integral equals that limit. In particular, if f has only finitely many discontinuities on [a,b], then f is Riemann integrable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This allows constructing integrability by excluding finitely many problematic points and using additivity/limits to cover the whole interval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changing values on a finite set doesn't affect integrability or integral (Proposition 5.2.10)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is Riemann integrable on [a,b] and g equals f except on a finite set S, then g is Riemann integrable and ∫_a^b g = ∫_a^b f.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses additivity and small intervals around changed points, showing their contribution can be made arbitrarily small.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotone functions are integrable (Proposition 5.2.11)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any monotone (increasing or decreasing) function on [a,b] is Riemann integrable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A uniform partition argument shows oscillation on each subinterval can be controlled and sum of oscillations goes to zero as mesh→0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Upper/lower-sum inequality for sums of bounded functions (Proposition 5.2.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: For bounded functions f,g on [a,b], one has ∫_a^b (f+g)_lower ≤ ∫_a^b f_lower + ∫_a^b g_lower and ∫_a^b (f+g)_upper ≥ ∫_a^b f_upper + ∫_a^b g_upper. (Inequalities for Darboux integrals; equalities require integrability.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows that sup/inf operations interact subadditively; helpful when f,g are not integrable to compare their Darboux integrals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Riemann sums and convergence criterion (exercises)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is Riemann integrable then uniform Riemann sums R_n (right, left, or midpoint with mesh→0) converge to ∫_a^b f. Conversely, there exist functions for which uniform Riemann sums converge but f is not Riemann integrable (exercise asks to construct such f).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises (e.g., 5.1.11) explore relationship between integrability and convergence of specific Riemann-sum approximations; useful as alternative practical tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical technique: choose partitions adapted to discontinuities/jumps
rubrics_metrics.description: In examples and exercises, integrability is often proved by taking partitions that isolate discontinuities (e.g., include points of jump) so that the contribution of bad intervals is controlled and U_P - L_P < ε.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the recurring construction used in examples: step functions, functions with finitely many jumps, and functions modified on finite sets.
